growth_story.headline: Qatar's income per person peaked in 2011 as its gas build-out ended, then shrank for over a decade as new LNG capacity stayed on hold and the population grew.
growth_story.arc: Qatar's income per person was lower in 2025 than in 1970, the first year of the record. It grew 2.1 percent a year from 1990 to 2003, then 5.6 percent a year from 2004 to 2011, when a long investment program to bring the country's natural resources to market culminated and income per person reached its peak. From 2012 to 2025 it shrank 2.0 percent a year, and by 2025 it stood 26.1 percent below the 2011 peak. The IMF linked the slowdown in 2012 to a self-imposed pause on adding LNG capacity, and later noted that large inflows of foreign workers drove high population growth. Falling hydrocarbon prices in 2014–16, a 2017 rift with Arab states that led to an embargo, and the 2020 pandemic were further shocks; growth averaged -1.0 percent a year over 2016–2025, against 1.1 over 2006–2015.

threads.title: Building out the gas fields
threads.text: The 2004–2011 era was the payoff of a long investment program to bring Qatar's natural resources to market. The IMF describes that program as culminating in 2011, the year income per person peaked.

threads.title: A pause on new gas
threads.text: Qatar held back further development of its North Field gas field until early 2017, so LNG capacity stopped growing. The IMF tied the slowdown in 2012 to this pause.

threads.title: Price falls, a rift, a pandemic
threads.text: Hydrocarbon prices fell in 2014–16, and in 2017 a diplomatic rift with Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain and Egypt led to an embargo against Qatar that was resolved only by 2021. The pandemic and a collapse in oil prices then brought a contraction in 2020, when income per person fell 8.9 percent, the steepest drop of the era.

growth_story.tension: The IMF said in 2019 that Qatar had absorbed the 2014–16 price fall and the 2017 rift, yet income per person fell every year from 2012 to 2019. More recently the IMF reported growth recovering in 2024 and 2025, while income per person fell 4.2 percent in 2024 and 1.1 percent in 2025. A growing population would explain the gap, but the recent sources do not say so.
